'''Maximilian Jacob Herzberger''' (7 or 17 Mar 1899, [[Berlin]], Germany — 9 Apr 1982, [[New Orleans]], United States)<ref name="geni.com">[http://www.geni.com/people/Max-Herzberger/6000000001854579784 Record] at geni.com, and related records</ref><ref name="goudsmit"/> was a German-American [[mathematician]] and [[physicist]], known for his development of the [[superachromat]] lens.

==Life==
Maximilian Herzberger was the son of Leopold Herzberger (born 7 Mar 1870, [[Krefeld]] — died in [[Rochester (NY)]]) and Sonja/Sofia Behrendt/Berendt/Berends (22 Mar 1876, Petersburg (Germany){{clarify|reason=As of today, no such town or village could be found. Maybe the source, viz. the geni.com page on Sonja Behrendt, is incorrect here.|date=February 2015}} — 28 Jan 1945, [[Florence]]); he had a sister Olga (24 Sep 1897, Berlin — 2 Aug 1922, Berlin). The family was [[Jewish]].<ref>[http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/Herzberger.html Maximilian Jacob Herzberger]</ref>
He studied mathematics and physics at the [[Berlin University]], where [[Albert Einstein]] was one of his professors, and later became a friend and advisor.<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|57r}}
In 1923, Herzberger finished his Ph.D. thesis ''Ueber Systeme hyperkomplexer Grössen'' under [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] and [[Issai Schur]] at the philosophical faculty.<ref>[http://edoc.hu-berlin.de/docviews/abstract.php?lang=ger&id=26997 Record] at Humboldt University Berlin</ref>
In 1925, he married Edith Kaufmann (10 Oct 1901, [[Stuttgart]] — 16 Feb 2001, [[Carlsbad (California)]] or [[New Orleans]]);
they had three children, born in Jena, viz. Ruth (born 1928), [[Ursula Bellugi]] (1931), and Hans (6 Aug 1932, spouse of [[Radhika Herzberger]]).<ref name="geni.com"/><ref name="goudsmit">[http://goudsmit.home.xs4all.nl/CollateralFamiliesPersonsV2/ps06_469.htm Person sheet] at goudsmit.home.xs4all.nl</ref>
No later than Sep 1930, he was assistant of [[Hans Boegehold]],<sup>([[:de:Hans Boegehold|de]])</sup> the chief of calculation office at [[Carl Zeiss AG|Carl Zeiss Jena]].<ref name="medicusbooks.com"/>

In 1934, the [[Nazis]] deprived him from his professorship at [[Jena University]] and his contract with Zeiss. Leaving Germany with a "total of $10 in my pockets".,<ref name="Dureau" /> he went initially to the Netherlands, where he was hosted by the Dutch physicist [[Bram van Heel|A.C.S. van Heel]].<ref>Inscription in first edition "Modern Geometrical Optics" found in A.C.S. van Heel's library: "To my friend A.C.S van Heel, who so generously helped me, when I had to flee Nazi Germany, Max Herzberger".</ref> After the [[Nazi occupation of the Netherlands]], he emigrated with his family to [[Rochester (NY)]],<ref name="medicusbooks.com">[http://www.medicusbooks.com/1-Autographen/Autographen/ALS-Optik/Boegehold-Hans-Herzberger-Max-MS-LS-Hektrographiertes-Typoskript-mit-zahlreichen-eigenhaendigen-Korrekturen-von-Herzberger-Dazu-ein-Brief-mit-beider-Unterschrift::2444.html Catalog entry] at medicusbooks.com, about a common letter of Boegehold and Herzberger to [[Erwin Lihotzky]] at the [[Leica Camera|Ernst Leitz GmbH]]</ref>
where he became head of [[Eastman Kodak]]'s optical research laboratories, arranged by Einstein.<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|57r}}
In 1940, he and his family became U.S. citizens.<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|58l}}
In 1945, he got the [[Cressy Morrison]] Award of the [[New York Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|57l}}

In 1954 he finished the development of the [[superachromat]] as the ultimately well-corrected lens for Kodak.<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|58m}}<ref>Herzberger, M., and N. McClure, [http://www.opticsinfobase.org/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-2-6-553 ''The design of superachromatic lenses''], ''[[Appl. Opt.]]'' Vol.2, pp.&nbsp;553–560 (June 1963)</ref>
in 1959, he was part of the inaugural class of Fellows of the Optical Society of America.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Max Herzberger {{!}} Optica |url=https://www.optica.org/History/Biographies/bios/Max_Herzberger |access-date=2024-09-09 |website=www.optica.org}}</ref> In 1962, he was awarded the [[Frederic Ives]] Medal of the [[Optical Society of America]].<ref>[http://www.opticsinfobase.org/josa/abstract.cfm?uri=josa-53-6-657 ''Maximilian J. Herzberger Frederic Ives Medalist for 1962''], [[JOSA]], Vol. 53, Issue 6, pp. 657-657 (1963)</ref><ref name="osa">{{cite web|url=http://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/awards/award_description/ivesquinn |title=Frederic Ives Medal / Quinn Prize - Awards - OSA.org &#124; The Optical Society |publisher=osa.org|accessdate=2015-02-14}}</ref>
In 1965, he retired from his position at Kodak, and helped building a graduate institute for optics in Switzerland,<ref name="Dureau"/>{{rp|58r}}
until in 1968 he followed invitation of the [[University of New Orleans]] to teach at their Physics Department.<ref name="Dureau">Lorena Dureau, [http://www.davidbellugi.com/herzberger/Max_article_enstein_protege.pdf ''Einstein's Protege''], p.56-58, Sep.???? (1970 or after)</ref>{{rp|57m,58r}}<ref name="medicusbooks.com"/>

He held patents for an ''"apochromatic telescope objective having three air spaced components"'',<ref>Oct. 1946 with Harvey O Hoadley, [https://patents.google.com/patent/US2487873 US 2487873] at google patents</ref> and a ''"superachromatic objective"''.<ref>May 1965 with Nancy R Mcclure, [https://patents.google.com/patent/US3395962 US 3395962] at google patents</ref> He died on 9 April 1982.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/04/12/obituaries/maximillian-herzberger-dies-einstein-s-student-and-friend.html|title=Maximillian Herzberger Dies; Einstein's Student and Friend|author=[[United Press International]]|date=April 12, 1982|page=B8|work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>
